_about: OUR recommendations, which are opinion and shown only when the reader turns on picks. Generated by tools/import_picks.py from data-src/picks_sf.csv; edit the CSV, not this file. verdict: "egg" (Golden Goose Egg, positive), "honk" (Certified HONK, negative) or "note" (an unrated Goosebase take; on a measure, `lean` gives the direction). For a measure, egg = YES and honk = NO. For offices, `target` names the candidate; a note without a target is a contest-wide take. Schema: docs/data-model.md.

us-rep-14.reasoning: Two Democrats. Wahab, the state senator, has the progressive groups behind the campaign (East Bay DSA, relaying California DSA, and the East Bay Young Dems); Hernandez has none of the groups we track. We lean Wahab.

ala-member-of-city-council-2-fremont.reasoning: The incumbent, endorsed by Ro Khanna and Alex Lee, running on parks, roads and climate. Parker runs on homelessness, police staffing and bringing businesses back. We lean Campbell.

ala-member-of-city-council-3-fremont.reasoning: Appointed in 2024 and running to keep the seat, with backing from Ro Khanna, Fiona Ma and Alex Lee. Sharma pitches an independent, evidence-based approach but hasn't filed a campaign committee. Low-information race; we lean Kimberlin.

ala-member-of-city-council-4-fremont.reasoning: Akbari runs on affordable housing and green space and has the broadest donor base in the race: about 160 donors under Fremont's $850 limit. Li has raised the most, but roughly $68K of the $110K is Li's own money. We lean Akbari.

ala-ac-transit-district-director-ward-3.reasoning: We'd normally back the experienced director, but AC Transit's outside investigator found Joel Young violated the district's gender-based harassment policy by grabbing fellow director Sarah Syed from behind at a 2025 event (Young says it was meant as support). Valencia has YIMBY Action, the East Bay Young Dems and the Alameda County Democrats. We lean Valencia.

ala-ac-transit-district-director-ward-4.reasoning: The incumbent. With AC Transit facing a projected $50M-a-year deficit and possible service cuts, we'd rather keep experienced directors. Syed survived a 2025 censure attempt over emails to staff (the board chose coaching instead); nothing we found changes our lean. We lean Syed.

ala-ac-transit-district-director-ward-5.reasoning: The incumbent and the board's vice president; experience matters with the agency's budget in trouble. Heads up: Grcar is on the ballot for five offices at once and Reynoso for three. We lean McCalley.

ala-bart-director-district-4.reasoning: The incumbent since 2010, backed by YIMBY Action and the East Bay Young Dems, and we found no press that changes that. Reynoso is also running for two other offices. We lean Raburn.

ala-alameda-county-water-district-direct.reasoning: We like an engineer on the water board: Miguel is a water district engineer, challenging incumbent Judy Huang. We lean Miguel.
We lean Paul Sethy, the incumbent, over Fremont councilmember Yang Shao.

ala-east-bay-regional-park-district-dire.reasoning: The incumbent, backed by the East Bay Young Dems. We like incumbents on technical boards like this one. We lean Sanwong.

governor.reasoning: It's a dangerous time not to have someone committed to democratic integrity at the helm of the most powerful state in the union. Vote for the Democrat here.

lt-governor.reasoning: It's a dangerous time not to have someone committed to democratic integrity at the helm of the most powerful state in the union, and the lieutenant governor becomes acting governor whenever the governor is out of state or unable to serve. The lieutenant governor also casts the tie-breaking vote in the State Senate. Vote for the Democrat here.

secretary-of-state.reasoning: The Secretary of State runs California's elections. It's not worth the risk of electing someone from a party that is actively undermining confidence in elections across the country. Vote for the Democrat here.

controller.reasoning: The Controller is California's chief fiscal officer: it pays the state's bills and audits how the money gets spent. Same story as the top of the ticket: we're not handing the state's books to the party undermining democratic institutions. Vote for the Democrat here.

treasurer.reasoning: The Treasurer is the state's banker: it invests the state's money and sells its bonds. Low drama, but not worth the risk. Vote for the Democrat here. Heads up for renters: the landlord lobby (the California Apartment Association) put $75K behind Kounalakis.

attorney-general.reasoning: The Attorney General is California's top lawyer and its front line against federal attacks on voting. At Trump's Justice Department, Gates signed the federal lawsuit demanding Orange County's unredacted voter records. Hard pass. Vote for the Democrat here.

insurance-commissioner.reasoning: Two Democrats, and a real split for us. Ben Allen has the pro-housing groups (YIMBY Action, GrowSF) and California Environmental Voters, but also about $3.6M in outside money from environmental, business and homebuilder groups, and only 0.3% of his campaign's money comes from small donors. Jane Kim has labor and the Working Families Party behind her, and the CalChamber's PAC has spent $1.5M attacking her. This office regulates home insurance, which matters for housing. We lean Kim: we love a populist and we're wary of that much outside money.

boe-2.reasoning: Two Democrats, for a board that lost most of its job in 2017, when sales-tax collection and most tax appeals moved to new agencies. It now mostly handles property, insurance and alcohol tax matters. Lieber is the incumbent, backed by SF Dems and the Pissed Off Voters; Pimentel has GrowSF and more money. Low stakes. We lean Lieber.

us-rep-11.reasoning: We dislike both candidates in this race for different reasons. Scott is more likely to follow mainstream national progressives, but is a bit too close to tech money for our taste.

We dislike both candidates in this race for different reasons. The affordability crisis in SF and the Bay Area as a whole has one root cause: housing. Local districts and neighborhoods don't have a good track record of allowing the kinds of housing we need, and Connie Chan seems to want to keep as much local control over housing policy as possible.

scotus-groban.reasoning: Yes, if you like Jerry Brown: Groban was Brown's senior advisor for seven years before Brown appointed Groban to the court in 2018.

scotus-evans.reasoning: Yes. The court's most frequent dissenter in criminal cases (66 dissents in the 2024-25 term, per the Daily Journal), often pushing for closer review of convictions. Before the bench, a federal court-appointed monitor of the Oakland Police Department.

We think that's the biggest issue in our education system right now. Heads up: starting in January 2027, most of this office's authority moves to a governor-appointed education commissioner. It still comes with a platform and a mouthpiece.

One of the two smallest campaigns in the race (about $7,000 raised); probably not a good use of your vote.

prop-1.reasoning: No argument against Prop 1 was even submitted. Vote yes.

prop-3.reasoning: Really only affects people making over $371K a year, and doesn't change the status quo. Vote yes.

prop-4.reasoning: We here at Goosebase support this because private financing of campaigns is a blight on society. We do, however, have reservations about the mechanics of these public funds. Vote yes.

prop-5.reasoning: California recalls are stupid as it is, and they can let someone without majority support replace the incumbent instead of holding a separate special election. Vote yes.

prop-37.reasoning: Adds fuel to housing demand without anywhere for that demand to go. It doesn't set the interest rate on these down-payment-replacing loans, and it props up home developers without enabling or requiring them to build where demand is highest. Vote no, for now.

prop-38.reasoning: A tough and misleading one. Without saying so outright, this measure all but guarantees that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy gets $4.2 billion (half the bond). We at Goosebase love science, but we also believe centralized decision-making outside of elected offices is a problem. Vote no.

prop-39.reasoning: Ridiculous additional barriers to voting that would cost tens to hundreds of millions of dollars a year. Vote no.

prop-40.reasoning: The tax is retroactive (it covers anyone who lived in California on January 1, 2026), so billionaires can't move to avoid it. Meta, for one, is already creating non-voting shares that can be sold without diluting Mark Zuckerberg's control; we read that as a way to raise cash for bills like this one. Vote yes and make them work for it.

prop-41.reasoning: Makes it harder to pass voter-approved taxes like a billionaire tax. We at Goosebase believe it should be easier to raise money for popular causes. Vote no.

prop-42.reasoning: Designed to make taxes like Prop 40 impossible in the future. Again, make the billionaires work for it. Vote no.

prop-43.reasoning: Makes it harder to pass voter-proposed local taxes by raising the bar from a simple majority to two-thirds. We at Goosebase believe it should be easier to raise money for popular causes. Vote no.

prop-44.reasoning: A tough one to read through. It's a strict rule that might help the healthcare workers' union SEIU-UHW (the measure's sponsor) negotiate with employers, but it could also leave community clinics less wiggle room for upgrades. Tentative yes: overly strong unions would be a new problem for our generation, and we like new problems.

prop-45.reasoning: Another tough choice, balancing speed of construction against letting reviews and local communities assess the impacts of new construction. Voter beware: it doesn't only apply to housing, and the wording is vague enough that a data center could sue its way into the exemption. Current rules don't really have hard deadlines; Prop 45 sets them. We at Goosebase love public review, but hate scope creep and a lack of concrete deadlines a little bit more. Tentative yes.

rtm.reasoning: It sucks that it's a regressive tax, but we can't afford to let transit go underfunded. Vote yes.

prop-a.reasoning: This one sucks; it's government minutiae. It bundles several Charter (i.e., SF's constitution) changes: 1. It eliminates, merges or moves some commissions out of the Charter and into city law (more Board of Supervisors control, and you still vote for those folks). 2. It lets the Board of Supervisors approve legal settlements more easily (by resolution instead of ordinance). 3. It creates a task force that meets every ten years to review the commissions. Tentative yes, because it doesn't move power into the executive. We're going to try to provide a summary table because this shit is confusing.

prop-b.reasoning: We love having a publicly controlled source of capital for loans. Vote yes.

prop-d.reasoning: Do you hate reading all these measure summaries? This would make citizen measures four times harder to qualify: from 2% to 8% of voters' signatures (about 10,600 to 42,500). Is that a bad thing? Supporters don't think so, and the measure gives up the mayor's own power to place measures directly as a carrot. We think this is a fake reduction in executive power and a real reduction in regular people's ability to propose changes to the city charter. Vote no.

prop-e.reasoning: Extends the mayor-appointed City Administrator's term to 10 years (from five), which spans multiple mayors, and gives the office broad power over spending and technology. Big increase in executive power. Tentative no.

prop-f.reasoning: More government minutiae, but this time about the mayor's power: way more control over departments, including hiring and firing commission and department heads. This is actually a function we think should live under the executive, moderated by not approving all the other increases in executive power. Tentative yes.

prop-g.reasoning: Leave the park alone. Vote no.

prop-h.reasoning: All the homies love Muni. Also, all the homies rent.

prop-i.reasoning: Tentative no. Locks half of the transfer-tax revenue from $10M+ property sales into specific housing initiatives and limits the Board's ability to change the tax. We at Goosebase generally don't like guaranteed spending (unless it's trains) because the demands of governance change.

prop-j.reasoning: Taxes lenders that foreclose on properties (commercial and larger residential buildings; homes with fewer than five units stay exempt). Vote yes.
